problem: Prior DRL ObjNav agents use object semantics/spatial context only from the current frame (or a few stacked frames / LSTM), ignoring the long-term temporal order of previously observed objects and scenes, so they get stuck in loops and deadlocks and take inefficient paths.
motivation: ObjNav is long-horizon and the target is often not visible at the start; views can be uninformative (e.g. a white wall). Long-term memory of observed objects should help the agent avoid loops and choose efficient routes, but RNNs handle long-range ordering poorly.
key_idea: Store a ring buffer of per-step scene features and object-context grids (Object-Scene Memory) and let a Transformer with temporal encoding, conditioned on the target word, attend over this history to feed an A3C policy.
insight: Long history alone is not enough: removing temporal encoding gives the largest drop (32 hist: SR 69.39→59.69, SPL 27.51→21.95), showing ordering of memory is vital. Longer memory (32) gives the best SPL (27.51) via more efficient paths, while short memory (4) gives best SR. Surprisingly, object-only inputs (w/o Scene) still reach SR 62.30–65.59, comparable to the LSTM baseline. Qualitatively, long memory lets the agent detect deadlocks and escape.
method: Feature Extractor: frozen ResNet-50 gives 2048-d scene feature from a 400x300 RGB image; word2vec gives 300-d target embedding; object context grid (16x16) holds cosine similarity between the target and detected objects at box centers, using GT labels/boxes.
Object-Scene Memory (OSM): ring buffer of the last T scene features and object grids; networks f_v, f_o, f_m fuse each entry into a 300-d vector m_t.
Temporal Encoding: sinusoidal encoding of the memory slot position added to the fused features, so the Transformer knows observation order.
Transformer encoder-decoder: encoder self-attends over the memory (masking empty slots); decoder attends from the target word embedding to produce feature x (1 layer, 5 heads).
A3C controller: two FC layers output the action distribution and value; the policy is trained from scratch.
Reward: +5 on success, S_bbox (target box area ratio) when it is the episode's highest, and -0.01 per step otherwise.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (frozen, pretrained) + word2vec (frozen) + Transformer + A3C (trained from scratch with RL)
setting.training_data: RL in 80 AI2-THOR rooms (20 each of kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom), 25M frames, 80 threads, 4 V100 GPUs
setting.observation: first-person RGB 400x300 plus GT object labels and bounding boxes
setting.action_space: discrete: Move Forward/Backward/Left/Right (0.5 m), Rotate L/R (45°), Look Up/Down (30°), Done
setting.privileged: GT object labels and bounding boxes for all objects in view (from the simulator)

numbers.eval_set_note: 20 unseen rooms (5 per category); 250 episodes per target class; 300-step limit

numbers_note: Custom AI2-THOR ObjNav benchmark (not Habitat); split is the 20 held-out rooms, mapped to val-unseen. No standard-benchmark results.
results: OMT reaches SR 69.4–71.1% and SPL 26.7–27.5%, beating the Druon et al. baseline (SR 61.55, SPL 20.83) and its 3-layer LSTM variant (63.25 / 23.96). It also exceeds the reported SR of Qiu et al. (65.3) and Du et al. (69.3), though their settings differ.
limitations: Relies on ground-truth object labels and bounding boxes rather than a real detector
Evaluated only in AI2-THOR with hand-picked target classes and small unseen rooms; comparison to SOTA is in non-identical settings
Absolute SPL is low (~27%) and no real-robot validation
builds_on: Druon et al. 2020 (object context grid ObjNav)
compares_to: Druon et al. 2020 baseline and LSTM variant
